passage: Two stories are told about the anger that seems to pervade online discussion, and each is convenient for someone. In the first, the ranking systems that decide what appears in a feed have manufactured outrage, turning otherwise reasonable people into combatants. In the second, told chiefly by those who build such systems, a feed merely reflects its users: it shows people what they engage with, and if what they engage with is furious, the fault lies in human nature, not in the code. The first story flatters users, who become the victims of a machine; the second flatters engineers, who become the neutral servants of a public. Neither is quite right.

Against the first story, it must be granted that outrage is old. Pamphleteers, broadsheets and street-corner orators discovered long before any computer that indignation sells, and audiences have always lingered over a scandal longer than over the correction that followed it. A ranking system that favours whatever holds attention did not invent this appetite. It found the appetite already there, and it could hardly have succeeded so quickly if it had not. Any account that treats the present climate as wholly unprecedented must therefore explain why the appetite it deplores appears so reliably in the commercial history of every earlier medium of mass communication.

But the second story trades on an ambiguity in the word 'want'. A feed ranked by engagement learns what people react to: what they click, what they pause over, what they reply to in anger. Reaction is not the same as endorsement. A person may linger over a provocative post in the way a driver slows to look at an accident, and may say, if asked afterwards, that she wishes she had seen less of such material. A system that learns only from the lingering will give her more of it, and will describe the result as giving her what she wants. It is giving her what she wanted in the moment of reaction, which may be the opposite of what she wants on reflection.

The older media of indignation differed in a further way that the mirror story overlooks. A newspaper editor chose what to print, but the feedback that reached him was slow and coarse, a matter of sales figures and letters to the editor. A feed reports, to every person who publishes in it, exactly how each post performed, often within minutes. Those who write for such an audience learn quickly which tone is rewarded, and many adjust accordingly, not because they are cynical but because they would like to be read. The ranking system therefore does not merely distribute a fixed supply of anger; it shapes the supply, by teaching producers what pays. A mirror that trains the face in front of it is not a mirror.

It does not follow that the remedy is simply to rank posts by what people say, on reflection, that they value. Reflective preferences are harder to measure, easier to misreport and, when a platform infers them, open to the charge that the platform has substituted its own judgement for the user's. These are real objections, and they counsel modesty about any redesign. But they cut both ways. A system that optimises for momentary reaction has also made a judgement about what its users really want; it has simply made that judgement silently, and in favour of the version of the user that is easiest to count. Neutrality, in this domain, is not an available option; the only choice is between an explicit conception of the user's interests and an implicit one.

options.B: arguing that engagement ranking neither invents outrage nor simply mirrors it, but amplifies an old appetite and reshapes its supply.

passage: Anyone who watches visitors in a busy gallery will notice how briefly most pictures are looked at. A few seconds for the image, a little longer for the label, and the visitor moves on. In response, many museums now promote what is sometimes called slow looking: sessions in which participants are invited to sit before a single work for a quarter of an hour or more, noting whatever comes to their attention. The premise is simple and attractive. We miss what is in paintings because we do not give them time, and if we gave them time, they would show us more.

The practice has real merits, and its critics should concede them. It interrupts the habit, encouraged by crowded rooms and handheld screens, of treating a picture as something to be recognised and ticked off. It gives permission to stay, which many visitors seem to need. And it does sometimes yield discoveries: a figure in the background that had gone unnoticed, a repeated colour that ties distant parts of the canvas together. But the premise behind it, that duration by itself turns into perception, is weaker than it looks. Fifteen minutes in front of a canvas can be fifteen minutes of reverie, of thinking about lunch, or of staring with growing unease at a surface that refuses to become interesting. Time is a condition of seeing, not a cause of it.

What turns time into seeing is a question. The art historian who notices in a moment that the light in a landscape falls from two directions does not see faster because her eyes are better; she sees because she has learned to ask where the light comes from, and the painting answers. Expertise, in this sense, is a stock of questions that direct the eye, questions that are not mysterious endowments but are acquired, often laboriously, through the comparison of many works, and that can therefore in principle be taught. This explains why experts often see in seconds what a patient beginner misses in an hour. The beginner is not looking less; he is looking without a question, and an unguided gaze tends to settle on whatever is largest, brightest or most familiar.

Yet the expert's advantage carries a risk of its own, and here the advocates of slow looking have a point that their own premise obscures. A stock of questions is also a stock of expectations. The historian who knows what to look for in a painting of a certain school may stop looking once she has found it, filing the picture under its category and failing to notice what does not fit. Questions direct the eye, but they also tell it where it need not go. Some of the most valuable observations a viewer can make come from setting expertise aside long enough to be surprised, and slow looking at its best is precisely a technique for producing that suspension.

The two halves of the matter therefore need each other. Time without questions drifts; questions without time confirm what they expected. Neither ingredient is dispensable, and neither, taken in isolation, is sufficient for the kind of perception that the advocates of slow looking rightly prize. The most useful practice is neither the patient blankness that slow looking sometimes encourages nor the quick classification that expertise permits, but an alternation between them: a period of asking, a period of letting the asking lapse, and a return to the picture to see whether it has said something the questions did not predict.

passage: Few things in a museum are read as often, or looked at as little, as the wall label. Visitors approaching a painting frequently read the small panel beside it first, glance at the picture to confirm what they have been told, and move on. Curators have noticed this pattern for a long time, and it has produced two opposite reactions. One camp argues that labels should be shortened or removed altogether, so that the visitor is thrown back onto the object. The other argues that labels should be expanded, written in friendlier language and supplemented with audio guides and screens, since a public that does not know what it is looking at cannot be expected to care.

Both reactions treat the label as though its only variable were quantity. The purist assumes that less text means more looking, but a visitor confronted by an unexplained altarpiece does not usually begin to look harder; more often she feels excluded and walks faster. The expansionist assumes that more text means more understanding, yet a long label that rehearses the artist's biography, the patron's family and the painting's later owners gives the visitor a great deal to know and very little to see. In each case the label is imagined as a container of facts, and the only argument is over how full the container should be.

A better question is what the label asks the visitor to do. A label can close a picture, by telling the viewer what it means, or it can open it, by directing attention to something that can be checked against the canvas itself. Compare two sentences about the same imagined portrait. The first says that the sitter was a wealthy merchant who commissioned the work to celebrate his marriage. The second says that the merchant's left hand rests on a ledger while his right holds his wife's glove, and invites the reader to decide which hand the painter has lit more brightly. The first sentence can be absorbed without raising one's eyes; the second cannot be finished without looking.

None of this means that historical information is a distraction. A viewer who does not know that a certain blue, ground from a semi-precious stone, was once among the costliest materials a painter could buy will miss part of what a patron was displaying when he asked for a sky full of it, and no amount of attentive looking will supply that fact. The point is that information earns its place on the wall when it changes what the visitor notices. Facts that merely sit beside the object, however accurate, belong in the catalogue, where they can be read at leisure by those who want them. The wall is too valuable, and the visitor's attention too brief, to be spent on anything else.

passage: Discussions of social capital commonly distinguish two kinds of tie. Bonding ties link people who are alike in some respect that matters to them, such as kinship, faith, neighbourhood or trade, and they supply loyalty and mutual help. Bridging ties link people across such lines, and they supply information, opportunities and the habit of dealing with strangers. Having drawn the distinction, many writers proceed to rank the two. Bridging is cast as the civic virtue that open societies need; bonding is regarded with suspicion, as the stuff of cliques, favouritism and inward-looking communities. The ranking is attractive partly because it flatters an ideal of openness, and partly because the dangers of tight-knit groups are so easy to picture, whereas their quieter contributions rarely make news.

The ranking is too quick. Consider a family that moves to a city where it knows no one except a handful of people from its home district. Those people find it a room, lend it money, explain which offices to visit and which employers pay on time. They are bonding ties in the purest sense, and without them the family might never acquire the stability from which wider contacts become possible. The first job outside the community, or the first friendship with a neighbour of a different background, frequently comes through someone who was met by way of the close circle. In such cases bonding is not the rival of bridging but its precondition.

It does not follow that close groups are always benign. The same density of ties that allows a community to support its members allows it to watch them, and the help it offers can come with a demand for conformity: marry within, trade within, think as we do. A young woman who wishes to train for an occupation the group disapproves of may find that the network which once sustained her family now stands in her way, and that the price of leaving it is the loss of everything it provided. Here the closeness that was a resource becomes a closure.

What separates the two cases is not the strength of the bonding ties but their permeability: whether membership of the close group is compatible with forming ties outside it, or is made conditional on refusing them. A policy that tried to weaken community networks in the name of integration would therefore risk destroying the very support that allows newcomers to reach beyond those networks in the first place. A better question to ask of any close group is not how tightly it binds but whether it lets its members go.

passage: Few rules of modern etiquette are enforced as fiercely as the ban on spoilers. A friend who reveals the ending of a film that you have not yet seen is treated as though he had stolen something from you, and online discussions of new releases now arrive wrapped in warnings. Behind the etiquette lies a theory about what stories are for. On this view, the value of a narrative is concentrated in the not-knowing, and once the outcome is known the thing is used up, like a lottery ticket that has already been scratched.

The theory is difficult to square with how people actually behave. Children demand the same bedtime story night after night and object loudly if a single word is changed. Adults rewatch favourite films until they can recite the dialogue, and they reread novels whose endings they could describe in a sentence. Audiences at tragedies drawn from well-known legends have always known that the hero will die; for centuries this knowledge did not stop them from attending, and it may even have been part of the attraction. If knowing the ending destroyed the pleasure, none of this would make sense.

What these cases suggest is that suspense is not simply uncertainty about outcome. A viewer can know perfectly well that the hero survives and still grip the arm of the chair when the rope begins to fray, because attention is absorbed in the unfolding moment rather than in a calculation about the final scene. Much of what we enjoy in a story, moreover, lies in the manner of its telling: the rhythm of a scene, the turn of a phrase, the way a minor character reveals himself in a single gesture. None of this is spoiled by a summary of the plot, since a summary is precisely what leaves it out.

It would be too much to conclude that spoilers do no harm at all. Some stories are built around a single reversal, and the shock of the first encounter with it is a real pleasure that cannot be had twice; a mystery whose solution has been announced in advance loses something that rereading does not restore. The etiquette, then, protects something genuine. But what it protects is a narrow and unrepeatable pleasure, not the whole value of a story, and a culture that treats the ending as the only thing worth guarding may gradually forget how to enjoy everything that comes before it.

passage: The traditional problem of other minds begins from an asymmetry. I am aware of my own pain directly, the argument runs, but I know of yours only through what you do: the wince, the cry, the hand withdrawn abruptly from the stove. How, then, am I entitled to believe that anything lies behind your behaviour at all? The classic reply is an argument from analogy. In my own case I observe that pain is regularly accompanied by wincing and crying; when I observe wincing and crying in you, I infer that pain is present in you as well, concealed from me but similar to my own.

Critics have long pointed out how fragile this inference is. It generalises from a single case to every other person, which is the kind of reasoning we would reject anywhere else: nobody who had examined one seed from a sack and found it fertile would conclude with any confidence that every seed in the sack would germinate. Worse, the conclusion can never be independently checked. In ordinary induction I can at least test a generalisation against further cases, but I can never step into your experience to confirm that the pain I inferred is really there.

These objections are sound, but they share the assumption they attack: that knowledge of other minds must be an inference from bodily movements to concealed inner states. That assumption does not describe how such knowledge actually arises. A child does not first register a contraction of facial muscles and then hypothesise distress; she sees that her mother is upset, and she sees it as immediately as she sees that the cup is full. Expressions are not evidence from which feelings are deduced. They are, in a great many cases, the very form in which feelings are visible to others, and to treat them as mere outward signs is to describe the face as a mask before asking what lies behind it.

None of this shows that we never reason about other minds. When a stranger's expressions are unfamiliar, when someone is deliberately concealing what she feels, or when we ask whether an octopus or a newborn experiences pain, we do weigh evidence and draw conclusions, and we can be badly wrong. But these are special cases, and they are intelligible only against a background in which most minds are simply seen. The sceptic's mistake is to take the hard case as the model for every case, and then to wonder why the model will not support the confidence we ordinarily have.

passage: Suppose a dozen firms bid for the right to drill in a tract of seabed whose reserves nobody knows, and that each firm commissions its own survey, and the surveys, being estimates, scatter around the true figure, some too high and some too low. If each firm bids what its own survey says the tract is worth, the contract will go to the firm whose survey was most optimistic, so that winning, in other words, is itself evidence of having overestimated. The firm that celebrates its victory has been selected for its error, and it will on average pay more than the tract is worth. This phenomenon is the winner's curse, and the striking thing about it is that no bidder needs to be foolish for it to occur, since each estimate may be honest and, taken alone, unbiased.

The remedy, in principle, is simple: a bidder should ask not what the tract is worth given its survey, but what it is worth given its survey and given that it has won. The second question yields a lower number, and a bidder who answers it will shade its bid below the raw estimate, more sharply the more rivals there are, since the highest of many estimates is more likely to be inflated than the highest of a few. Shading of this kind is not timidity but the correct response to a feature of the situation that the unconditioned estimate ignores.

A natural objection is that the curse should vanish with experience, because firms that overpay will lose money, notice and adjust, while those that do not will be driven from the market. There is truth in this, and seasoned bidders in many settings do shade their bids, but the learning is slower than the objection supposes. The outcome of any single auction is noisy, since a tract that disappoints may simply have been unlucky. Worse, the firms that lose never discover what the prize was really worth, so the information that would correct everyone's estimates is gathered only by the winners, and slowly. A lesson that must be extracted from a few expensive and ambiguous victories is not quickly learned.

For this reason the design of an auction matters as much as the wisdom of its participants. Formats in which bids are revealed as they rise allow each bidder to watch rivals drop out and to infer something about their estimates, and a bidder who can see how far others are willing to go has less reason to fear that its own enthusiasm is an error. Sealed bids, by contrast, leave each participant alone with a single survey and its uncorrected optimism. The point is not that one format is always superior, since open bidding has weaknesses of its own, among them the ease with which rivals can signal to one another, but that the curse is a property of the information structure, and so can be eased by changing that structure rather than by exhorting bidders to be cleverer.

passage: In most markets the price does the work of allocation. If more people want a good than there are units of it, the price rises until the excess disappears, and whoever is willing to pay the new price obtains the good. But there is a family of markets in which this mechanism cannot operate, because each side must choose the other. A university cannot simply admit whoever is willing to pay the most, nor can an applicant simply buy a place; a hospital hiring junior doctors cares which doctors it gets, and the doctors care which hospital they join. In such markets, sometimes called matching markets, a transaction requires mutual acceptance, and no single number can bring about a match that both sides want.

Left to themselves, matching markets tend to fail in characteristic ways. One is unravelling: because the strongest candidates are in demand, employers try to secure them by making offers earlier than their rivals, and the competition for earliness can push offers so far forward that they are made before anyone knows how good the candidates are. Another is congestion: when offers must be accepted or refused quickly, a candidate holding one offer may not learn in time of a better one, and the market clears without having considered all its possibilities. A third is strategic misrepresentation, in which participants conceal their true preferences, ranking a likely option first rather than the one they actually want, because they fear that revealing their real wishes will cost them.

The remedy that has often been adopted is not deregulation but construction: a clearinghouse to which both sides submit ranked lists, and which computes an assignment by a procedure known to have certain properties. The property most often sought is stability, meaning that there is no applicant and employer, not matched to each other, who would both prefer to be. A stable assignment removes the motive to break ranks, since no such pair can do better by striking a private deal, and with a suitable procedure at least one side can be given no reason to misreport its preferences. Such clearinghouses show that a market is not always a spontaneous order arising wherever people are free to trade; it can be an artefact, built to solve problems that freedom alone creates.

None of this means that design can substitute for the willingness of participants. A clearinghouse works only if enough of both sides join it, and an elegant procedure is useless if the most sought-after employers find it more profitable to recruit privately. Nor can a procedure deliver every desirable property at once: no procedure, for instance, can give both sides complete reason to report honestly while always producing stable outcomes. The designer chooses among imperfect options, and the choice reflects judgements about whose interests deserve protection. The engineering of markets is thus a political as well as a technical art, but it is an art that can be practised well or badly, and the difference matters to the people whose lives it arranges.

passage: In most schools a test is understood as a thermometer. It is applied at the end of a period of learning to find out how much has been learned, and like a thermometer it is supposed to leave the thing it measures unchanged. The understanding is so familiar that it seldom occurs to anyone that it might be false. Yet one of the more robust findings in the psychology of memory is that the act of retrieving something from memory is not a neutral reading: it changes the memory, and generally strengthens it, so that material which has been recalled once is more likely to be recalled again than material which has merely been seen again.

The contrast is clearest when the two activities are set against each other. Suppose two groups of students study the same passage, after which one group rereads it while the other closes the book and writes down whatever it can remember. The design holds constant both the material and the time spent on it, so that the only difference between the groups is whether they looked at the passage again or tried to bring it back unaided. Tested a few minutes later, the rereaders often do as well or better; tested a week later, the group that practised recall tends to remember considerably more. The advantage of retrieval, in other words, is easily hidden by the timing of the measurement, which may be one reason why it was overlooked for so long by teachers and students alike.

What is more striking is how little the students themselves sense any of this. Asked to predict their own performance, rereaders tend to be the more confident group. Rereading produces a feeling of fluency, in which the sentences are familiar and slide past easily, and ease of processing is readily mistaken for mastery. Attempting recall produces the opposite feeling, since it is effortful, it exposes gaps and it is often unpleasant, which is presumably why students left to themselves so rarely choose it. Teachers are not immune to the same illusion, since a class that has just reread its notes looks, and feels, better prepared than one that has just struggled to recall them. The method that feels like learning and the method that produces it are, at least here, not the same, and the lesson generalises uncomfortably: a learner's own sense of how well a session went is an unreliable guide to how much it achieved.

It would be easy to draw from all this a crude conclusion, that schools should simply test more, but the finding does not support it. What strengthens memory is the effort of retrieval, not the apparatus of examination, and the apparatus can work against the effort. A high-stakes test that provokes anxiety, or that is followed by no feedback, may teach students little except to fear tests, and a wrong answer recalled confidently and never corrected may itself be strengthened. The useful practice is humbler than the word 'test' suggests: it consists of frequent, low-stakes attempts to recall, each followed by a chance to check, built into ordinary study. None of this requires abolishing examinations, which serve purposes of certification that have little to do with memory; it requires only that they not be mistaken for the whole of what testing can do. Understood in this way, the thermometer turns out to be one of the more effective means of raising the temperature it was meant only to record.

passage: Few moral injunctions are now repeated with more confidence than the injunction to remember. After a civil war, a dictatorship or a period of communal violence, it is taken almost for granted that the truth must be told, the dead named and the guilty identified, and that a society which declines to do so is building its future on a lie. The case for this view is strong, and nothing that follows is meant to deny it. Those who suffered have a claim to be believed, and a society that teaches its children a false account of its own recent past does them a lasting harm. But the view carries an assumption that deserves examination: that remembering, in public and in detail, is always what allows former enemies to go on living side by side.

The historical record is less obliging than the injunction. A number of societies, ancient and modern, have made peace by agreeing, in one form or another, not to reopen the wrongs of the conflict just ended. Such agreements are often described as attempts at forgetting, but the description is misleading. No decree can make people forget what they suffered or what they did, and none of these arrangements tried to. What they established was something narrower: a rule about the public use of the past. Past crimes would not be prosecuted, or not beyond a certain point; old grievances would not be made the basis of political campaigns; the question of who had done what to whom would, for a time, be kept out of the courts and the assemblies, even as it continued to be remembered in kitchens and graveyards.

Whether such a rule is wise seems to depend less on the principle involved than on timing. In the first years after a conflict, when the losing side still has the means to fight and the institutions of the new order are fragile, a full public reckoning may reopen the war it is meant to close, and the people most likely to pay for that are the ones a reckoning was supposed to vindicate. A generation later, the balance may look quite different. The armed men have grown old, the institutions have settled, and the children of those who suffered may reasonably ask why the silence that once protected the peace should still protect those who did the harm.

For the costs of silence do not fall evenly. The perpetrator who is spared prosecution gains something definite; the victim who is asked not to speak of what was done gives something up, and is often asked to do so by people who lost far less. A peace that rests indefinitely on such an asymmetry is unlikely to remain a peace in any full sense. It may endure as an arrangement while decaying as a settlement, leaving resentments that later politicians find all too easy to exploit.

The upshot is that agreed silence should be judged neither as a betrayal of memory nor as a model of wisdom, but as a provisional arrangement whose legitimacy depends on what happens to it later. A silence that a society chooses, and later chooses to break, may have served both peace and justice in their turn. The worst outcome is not silence as such but a silence that becomes permanent by default, that no one ever decides to keep, and that is mistaken, by those who benefit from it, for a consensus that was never actually reached.

passage: It has become a commonplace that the metaphors buried in ordinary speech reveal the structure of ordinary thought. We speak of arguments as if they were battles, defending positions, attacking weak points, winning or losing; we speak of time as if it were space, with deadlines approaching, holidays behind us and the future ahead. On the view that has made this observation famous, such expressions are not decorations added to a literal meaning but the surface of deep conceptual mappings, in which one domain of experience is understood in terms of another. We do not merely talk about argument as war; to a large extent, it is claimed, we think about it that way, and we would argue differently if our language had taught us to think of it as, say, a dance.

The opposing view is equally simple. Most of these expressions, it holds, are dead metaphors, idioms whose figurative origin is no longer felt by anyone who uses them. A speaker who says that a table has legs is not thereby thinking of the table as an animal, and a speaker who defends a position need not have soldiers anywhere in mind. On this account, inferring a mental mapping from a pattern of idioms is like inferring a belief in sorcery from the fact that people say 'bless you' after a sneeze: the history of an expression is mistaken for its present psychology.

Each view, I think, gets one thing right and one thing wrong. The sceptic is right that the evidence most often cited for the mapping view is weaker than it looks. If the existence of the mapping is inferred from the expressions, and the expressions are then explained by the mapping, the argument has gone round in a circle; the sheer number of warlike expressions for argument cannot by itself show that anything in the mind corresponds to them. But the sceptic is wrong to treat these expressions as a collection of fossils. Dead metaphors are inert: one cannot extend the legs of a table into talk of its knees or its gait and expect to be understood. The metaphors of argument and time are not inert in this way. A speaker who says that her opponent's case was all ammunition and no target, or that next week is already breathing down our necks, may be using a phrase she has never heard, and she is understood at once. Something is generating these extensions, and a list of frozen idioms cannot be it.

Productivity, then, rather than frequency, is the better test of whether a metaphor is alive, and by that test many everyday metaphors are alive, at least in the sense that speakers can use them as patterns for making and understanding new expressions. That is a real result, and it is more than the sceptic allows. It is also less than the mapping view claims. To show that a pattern is available for making expressions is not to show that it governs how people reason when they are not speaking, still less that a different language would leave them reasoning differently. Those further claims are empirical, and they can be settled only by evidence that does not itself consist of the very expressions in question: by watching how people solve problems, judge situations or remember events, and asking whether the metaphor leaves its mark there.

The debate has often been conducted as though one had to choose between seeing language as a window onto thought and seeing it as a heap of dead habits. The more modest position is less exciting but easier to defend: our metaphors are living tools of expression, and their influence on thought beyond expression is an open question that the metaphors themselves cannot answer.

passage: In most human groups some people are listened to more than others, get their way more often and receive a larger share of whatever the group values. Students of status have long suspected that this single word conceals two different arrangements. In one, a person rises because others fear him: he can hurt them, withhold what they need or make their lives difficult, and they defer in order to avoid those costs. In the other, a person rises because others want something from him that he gives freely, usually knowledge or skill, and they defer in order to stay close enough to learn. The first route is commonly called dominance and the second prestige, and an influential line of thought in evolutionary anthropology holds that the second is a distinctively human addition to an older primate inheritance.

The argument for that view rests on the peculiar importance of cultural learning in our species. A creature that acquires most of its survival skills by copying others faces a constant problem of whom to copy, and a strong incentive to secure access to the best models. Deference, on this account, is a kind of payment: the learner offers attention, praise, small services and a willingness to yield in disputes, and in return is tolerated at the elbow of the skilled. If the account is right, it explains why prestige is freely conferred rather than extracted, why prestigious people are approached rather than avoided, and why we find ourselves imitating not only what admired people do well but much else about them besides.

That last consequence deserves more attention than it usually receives, because it shows that prestige is not simply the benign twin of dominance. Imitation guided by prestige is broad and indiscriminate. A learner cannot always tell which of a successful person's habits are responsible for the success, and so tends to copy a bundle of them: the method, but also the dress, the opinions and the manner of speech. In a small community this overspill is cheap and may even be useful, since the bundle often travels together for good reasons. In a large society with mass media, it allows people who are prestigious in one domain to exert influence far outside it, and the deference they receive bears no relation to any competence they have in the matters on which they are now heeded.

There is a further complication. The two routes are clean in theory and tangled in practice. A person who gains prestige acquires allies, resources and a following, and these are exactly the instruments with which dominance is exercised; prestige can thus be converted into the power to coerce, and the conversion is not always visible to those who continue to admire. Conversely, a dominant figure may cultivate the outward marks of prestige, surrounding himself with displays of learning or generosity that make submission feel like admiration. Observers who ask simply whether a leader is feared or respected will often find that the honest answer is both.

None of this undermines the distinction; it is precisely because the two routes can be told apart in principle that their mixture in practice becomes something to look for. What it undermines is the comfortable assumption that a society which replaces dominance with prestige has thereby solved the problem of status. Prestige allocates influence according to perceived excellence, and perception can be managed. The practical question for any institution is therefore not whether it rewards prestige rather than force, which most modern institutions at least claim to do, but whether it keeps the deference people receive tied to the domain in which they have actually earned it.

passage: In the decades after the British Empire abolished slavery in the 1830s, sugar planters in colonies such as Mauritius, Trinidad and British Guiana, and later Fiji, turned to a different source of labour: indentured workers, most of them recruited in India, who signed contracts binding them to an estate for a fixed term of years. Ever since, the system has been argued over in terms set by the institution it replaced. Its critics have called it slavery under a new name; its defenders, at the time and since, have insisted that it was a form of voluntary migration, entered into by contract and ended by the contract's expiry. Each side treats the question as one of classification, as though the decisive task were to place indenture on the correct side of the line between slave and free.

There are good reasons to resist the first classification. Indentured workers were not property. They could not be sold, their children did not inherit their status, and at the end of the term many returned home, while others stayed, bought land and built communities whose descendants remain in those countries today. To call this slavery is to lose sight of what was specifically terrible about slavery, and it risks erasing the choices, however constrained, that migrants made. But the second classification fares no better. Recruits were often misled about the work and the wages that awaited them; many were illiterate and signed documents they could not read; and once on the estate they found that the contract, far from protecting them, was the instrument of their confinement.

This last point is the one that both classifications miss. Colonial labour laws typically made it a criminal offence, not merely a breach of contract, for an indentured worker to be absent from work, to leave the estate without a pass, or to refuse a task. A worker who walked away could be arrested, fined or imprisoned, and the time spent in prison might be added to the term he owed. The coercion, in other words, did not stand outside the contract and contradict it; it was written into the contract and enforced by courts. The language of free agreement and the reality of compulsion were not opposed but fused.

Seen this way, indenture is less a halfway house between slavery and freedom than a demonstration that the line between them was never as clean as abolitionists hoped. The abolition of property in persons did not by itself abolish compulsion; it moved compulsion into the law of contract, where it could be presented as the free choice of the person compelled. That is a lesson with uses beyond the nineteenth century. Wherever a worker's right to leave a job is restricted by debt, by the confiscation of documents or by a visa tied to a single employer, the question worth asking is not whether a contract exists, but what the contract permits others to do to the person who signed it.

passage: Physicists have long remarked that several of the numbers fixing the behaviour of matter seem oddly well suited to the existence of anything as complicated as a living thing. Were certain forces a little stronger or a little weaker, the argument runs, stars would burn out too quickly or never ignite, atoms heavier than hydrogen would be scarce, and chemistry would offer nothing as intricate as a cell. How tightly these numbers are really constrained is debated, and some claims of extreme precision have not survived scrutiny. Enough of the pattern has held up, however, to pose a question: why should the constants of nature fall within the narrow ranges that permit observers to exist at all?

One family of answers appeals to what is usually called anthropic reasoning. Its modest form makes a point that sounds almost too obvious to state: whatever we observe must be compatible with our being there to observe it. We should not be astonished to find ourselves on a planet with liquid water and a tolerable climate, since observers could hardly have arisen anywhere else; to treat our surroundings as a fair sample of the cosmos would be like concluding that a town's residents are unusually fit because everyone one has met there was met at the swimming pool. In this form the principle is not a theory of anything. It is a warning about bias, and as a warning it is both correct and useful.

The difficulty begins when the same reasoning is asked to explain the constants themselves. Consider a lottery. A winner who learns that millions of tickets were sold need suspect nothing: someone had to win, and the winner is simply whoever did. But if only one ticket was ever printed and it won, the winner's existence explains nothing about why that ticket was drawn; it guarantees only that, had it not been, there would be no winner left to wonder. A selection effect does explanatory work only when there are many draws among which selection can operate. Applied to the cosmos, anthropic reasoning dissolves the puzzle of fine tuning only if there are many universes, or many regions of one, in which the constants take different values, and we necessarily find ourselves in one of the hospitable few.

Defenders of the approach reply that such an ensemble is not invented for the purpose. Some cosmological theories, developed to address quite different problems, appear to imply a vast number of regions with differing properties, and if those theories are right, the anthropic explanation comes, so to speak, free of charge. The reply has force, but it shifts the burden rather than lifting it. The explanation is now exactly as good as the theory that supplies the ensemble, and since the other regions are, on most versions, unobservable in principle, the evidence for that theory must come from somewhere else. Anthropic reasoning cannot certify its own premise.

None of this shows that the approach is unscientific, a charge often levelled against it with more heat than precision. Selection effects are a respectable part of reasoning in every empirical science, and ignoring them produces errors as surely as overrating them does. The narrower lesson is that the modest principle and the ambitious one are different claims and should not borrow each other's credibility. The first is nearly beyond dispute and explains almost nothing on its own; the second would explain a great deal, but only on a condition that the principle itself is powerless to establish.

passage: Few proposals in development policy provoke as reliable a reaction as giving poor households money with no strings attached. The objection usually arrives before the argument has been heard: the money will be drunk, gambled or otherwise wasted. It is worth noticing how rarely this suspicion is applied to other recipients of public money: pensioners are not asked to show receipts, and a tax refund arrives without an accompanying lecture on how it ought to be spent. The worry is reserved for people whose poverty is taken, often without anyone saying so, as evidence that they cannot be trusted with choices.

The suspicion has been tested more often than its persistence would suggest. Evaluations of cash programmes in a range of poor countries have generally found little sign that recipients increase their spending on alcohol or tobacco, and many have found the money going to food, school costs, livestock, tools and the repair of homes. This should not be surprising, since a household living close to the margin knows its own most pressing constraint far better than an official in a distant ministry, and the constraint differs from one family to the next: a roof for one, a debt for another, a sewing machine for a third. A transfer in kind, or one tied to a particular use, has to guess, and it guesses the same thing for everyone.

None of this makes conditions pointless. Where the aim is a specific behaviour whose benefits fall partly on others, or arrive too late to weigh heavily with a hard-pressed parent, such as keeping a daughter in school or bringing an infant for vaccination, a condition can do work that cash alone may not. And in remote places where markets are thin, a sudden injection of money can push up the prices of the few goods available rather than raising what people can actually buy. These are genuine qualifications, and a careful designer of programmes will take them seriously; but they are reasons for attaching conditions in particular cases, argued on their merits, not grounds for a general presumption that the poor will misuse what they are given.

The practical upshot is a reversal of the burden of proof. The default should be cash, and anyone proposing to restrict its use should have to show what the restriction achieves and what it costs, including the cost of monitoring and the quieter cost of telling adults that they are not trusted. Paternalism is sometimes justified, and there will be programmes in which the case for it can be made convincingly; it should not, however, be the starting assumption.

passage: Few images of empire are as familiar as that of European diplomats bent over a map of Africa, ruler in hand, dividing a continent they had barely visited. The image is usually summoned to explain why so many of the continent's borders run in straight lines, and why so many of its states have struggled: the borders, it is said, were artificial, cutting across peoples and lumping together others who had nothing in common, and the conflicts of the post-colonial era are their bitter harvest. The story has the merit of placing responsibility where much of it belongs. As an explanation, however, it is weaker than its popularity suggests.

Begin with the image itself. The conference held in Berlin in 1884 and 1885 is often remembered as the moment of partition, but it chiefly agreed on rules by which European powers would recognise one another's claims. Most actual boundaries were settled afterwards, over decades, through bilateral treaties, exchanges of territory and survey commissions, and many of them followed rivers, watersheds or the limits of existing polities rather than lines of latitude. The straight lines are real, but they cluster in deserts and thinly populated regions, where they divided relatively few people.

More fundamentally, the charge of artificiality proves too much. Every border is artificial in the sense that people drew it, and many of the borders of Europe were fixed by wars, dynastic marriages and peace conferences no more attentive to local wishes than any colonial commission. If artificial borders caused instability by themselves, much of the world would be permanently at war. Nor is it obvious what a natural border would be. Peoples overlap, migrate and intermarry; a line that united one group would divide another. When African states gained independence, their leaders, aware of these difficulties, chose through the Organisation of African Unity to accept the boundaries they had inherited rather than reopen them, judging that an attempt to redraw them would be more dangerous than living with them.

None of this acquits the colonial powers. Boundaries were indeed drawn without consulting the people they affected, and some did separate communities from their pastures, markets and kin. But the more serious legacy lay inside the lines rather than in their placement: states built for extraction, with administrations designed to collect revenue and keep order rather than to represent, and with ethnic categories hardened by colonial policy into the main currency of politics. To blame the shape of the map is to look at the frame and miss the picture.

passage: The case for deciding by majority is usually made on grounds of fairness rather than wisdom. Majorities are not reliably right, but a procedure that counts each vote equally treats each voter as an equal, and no rival procedure seems to do so as well. There is a second, less often stated part of the case. Majority rule is tolerable to those who lose because losing is expected to be temporary. Today's minority may be tomorrow's majority, since coalitions shift as issues change, and a citizen who is outvoted on one question can reasonably expect to be on the winning side of another. Over time, the losses are spread around.

This second condition does not always hold. When the issues that matter most to people line up with a stable division in the society, by language, region or ancestry, for instance, the same group may find itself outvoted on question after question for generations. Its members cast their votes, and their votes are counted equally, but the counting never changes the result. Formal equality at the ballot box then coexists with something very like permanent exclusion. To tell such a minority that it has been treated fairly because each of its votes weighed as much as anyone else's is to mistake the form of fairness for its substance.

Various remedies have been proposed: requirements of supermajorities for certain decisions, the devolution of some powers to regions where the minority is concentrated, electoral systems that give smaller groups a share of seats, and constitutional rights that no majority may override. Each has costs. Supermajority rules protect minorities by making change difficult, which also protects whatever injustices the status quo contains. Devolution can create new minorities within the regions it empowers. Entrenched rights shift power from elected bodies to courts, whose members the minority usually has no means of holding to account.

None of these costs settles the matter, but together they suggest that the problem should be framed differently. The persistent minority is not evidence that majority rule is unjust in itself. It is evidence that one of the conditions under which majority rule is fair has failed. The aim of a remedy, accordingly, should be to restore that condition where possible, for example by encouraging cross-cutting associations that loosen the grip of a single division on political life, rather than to replace majority rule with a different principle of decision. Where the condition cannot be restored, stronger protections may be needed, but they should be understood as repairs to a damaged procedure, not as a rival theory of legitimacy.

passage: A familiar picture of scientific objectivity confines values to the edges of inquiry. Values may legitimately decide which problems are worth studying and how results are used, but in the central act of science, deciding whether the evidence supports a hypothesis, they are supposed to have no place. A researcher who lets personal hopes affect whether a conclusion is accepted is, on this picture, simply doing bad science, and the remedy is a stricter separation between the laboratory and the world outside it.

The trouble is that evidence rarely settles a question outright, and so accepting a hypothesis always involves deciding that the evidence is strong enough. How strong is strong enough? Consider a laboratory testing whether an industrial solvent damages the liver. If it wrongly concludes that the solvent is safe, workers may be harmed; if it wrongly concludes that the solvent is dangerous, a useful product may be withdrawn and money wasted. Which error is worse, and therefore how much evidence to demand before declaring the solvent harmful, is not something the data can decide. It depends on how one weighs injured workers against lost revenue, which is a question of value. Two laboratories examining identical data could therefore set the threshold in different places, and neither would have misread a single measurement.

A natural reply is that scientists need not accept or reject anything. They could report the probability that the hypothesis is true, given the evidence, and leave the decision to those who must act. The reply is attractive but harder to carry out than it sounds. Before any probability can be reported, the investigators must decide how to classify ambiguous tissue samples, which measurements to discard as faulty and which statistical model to fit, and each of these decisions can err in either direction, with the same uneven consequences. The weighing of errors does not disappear; it moves to a stage where it is less visible.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that anything goes. The argument shows that values can properly bear on how much evidence to require, given what is at stake if one is wrong. It does not show that values can bear on what the evidence is, or license a researcher to discount an inconvenient result because it is unwelcome. The distinction is between setting the bar and moving the evidence, and the integrity of science depends on keeping the two apart, not on pretending that the bar sets itself.

passage: For much of the last century, the standard official response to an informal settlement was to remove it. Planners looked at a hillside of self-built houses, narrow lanes and improvised water connections and saw a problem of housing quality, to be solved by demolition and the construction of orderly blocks elsewhere, usually on cheaper land at the edge of the city. The logic seemed humane as well as tidy: people living without drains or secure walls would be given drains and secure walls. That the residents frequently resisted, and that many of the new blocks were half empty within a few years, was read as ingratitude, or as evidence that the poor did not know their own interests.

A different reading is now more common, and it is more persuasive. An informal settlement is not simply a stock of poor dwellings; it is a working arrangement of livelihoods, and its location is usually its chief asset. A family that sells cooked food near a bus depot, a tailor who takes in work from a nearby market, a mother whose children attend a school within walking distance: all of them chose the site because of what it is close to. Relocation to a distant estate improves the walls while destroying the arrangement. The household may gain a toilet and lose two hours a day to travel, or lose the income that made the new rent payable at all. Seen this way, the empty blocks were not a puzzle but a verdict.

Upgrading in place starts from this recognition. Instead of replacing the settlement, it adds what is missing: paved lanes, drainage, water and sewer lines, street lighting and, crucially, some form of secure tenure, so that residents can invest in their houses without fearing that the next official survey will mark them for demolition. Because the residents remain where they are, the networks that sustain them survive, and the public money spent goes into infrastructure rather than into reproducing, at great cost and in the wrong place, a community that already existed.

None of this makes upgrading a universal remedy. Some settlements stand on land that floods every monsoon or slides in heavy rain, and to improve them in place is to invest in a future disaster. Nor is upgrading automatically benign: lanes widened for drainage can require the demolition of some houses, and a programme that installs pipes but withholds tenure leaves residents improved and still insecure. The case for upgrading is therefore not that informal settlements are good as they are, a romantic view their residents rarely share. It is that the people who built them understood something about the city that the planners who wished to clear them did not.

passage: For a time it was widely believed, among journalists and fact-checkers as much as among researchers, that correcting a false belief could make matters worse. The idea, which came to be called the backfire effect, held that people confronted with evidence against a cherished belief would not merely resist it but cling to the belief more tightly, as though the correction were an attack to be repelled. It had an intuitive appeal: most of us have argued with someone who seemed to grow more certain with every fact we offered. And it carried a discouraging moral. If correction backfires, perhaps it is better not to correct at all.

Subsequent research has been considerably kinder to correction. Larger studies, with more varied topics and more diverse participants, have generally found that people who receive a factual correction move, on average, towards the accurate view, even when the correction cuts against their political loyalties. Reversal of the kind the early findings described appears to be rare, and some of the original results have proved difficult to reproduce. The more careful conclusion is not that people are perfectly responsive to evidence but that they are responsive to it in the ordinary, imperfect way: they update, though often less than they should.

It is worth asking why the backfire idea spread so far on so slender a basis. Part of the answer is that it flattered a certain cynicism about the public, and part is that it confused resistance with reversal. Someone who hears a correction and does not change his mind has resisted it; someone who becomes more convinced of the falsehood has reversed. The first is common and unremarkable, since people rarely abandon a belief after a single encounter with contrary evidence. Only the second would justify the conclusion that correcting is counterproductive, and it is the second that the evidence has failed to find with any regularity.

This does not mean that correction is a cure. Its effects often fade over weeks, so that people drift back towards the belief they were talked out of, and accepting that a particular claim is false does not necessarily change the attitudes the claim was used to support. A voter may concede that a politician's statistic was wrong and still admire the politician exactly as much. These are serious limits, but they are limits of a different kind. They call for corrections that are repeated, that offer an alternative explanation rather than a bare denial, and that are not expected to carry more weight than a single fact can bear. They do not call for silence.

The history of the backfire effect is thus a small lesson about the life of findings as well as about belief. A striking result, especially one that confirms what people already suspect, can travel much faster than the slower work of checking it, and the effort to correct a mistaken finding meets the same ordinary resistance, though not reversal, that greets any correction.
